cards.front: Why do physical and chemical barriers matter before the immune system is needed?
cards.back: They act first and stop many pathogens entering or surviving, so the immune system does not need to recognise each one. Intact **skin** blocks entry, mucus traps microbes, and stomach acid kills many swallowed pathogens.
cards.hint: Think about what happens before any immune cell gets involved.

cards.front: How does a lymphocyte pick out one particular pathogen?
cards.back: Each lymphocyte has receptors with a particular binding shape. A matching **antigen** binds that receptor and can help activate the lymphocyte.

cards.front: How do innate and adaptive responses differ?
cards.back: Innate responses recognise broad **pathogen features** and act rapidly, with no antigen-specific memory. Adaptive responses use lymphocytes matching a specific antigen, develop more slowly in a first infection, and form memory cells.
A **molecule** recognised by a specific lymphocyte receptor or antibody. Different pathogens can carry different antigens.

cards.front: A student says an antigen is always a whole pathogen. What is wrong?
cards.back: An antigen is a **molecule**, or part of one, that can be recognised. It does not have to be a whole pathogen.

cards.front: Outline how an innate response deals with a pathogen that has crossed a barrier.
cards.back: 1 Damaged tissue and immune cells release signals that start **inflammation**. 2 Nearby blood vessels widen and become more permeable, letting defensive cells and proteins into the tissue. 3 Phagocytes move to the infection and engulf pathogens by **phagocytosis**, enclosing them in vesicles to be broken down.
A **tissue response** that increases blood flow and vessel permeability near injury or infection, bringing defensive cells and proteins in. Redness, warmth and swelling can result.
Immune cells that **engulf** particles, including pathogens, and break them down.

cards.front: How do B lymphocytes help defeat a pathogen?
cards.back: Activated B lymphocytes develop into **plasma cells** that release antibodies matching the antigen. Antibodies bind pathogens or their toxins, blocking their action or making them easier to remove.
cards.hint: Follow the chain from B cell to antibody.

cards.front: A student claims antibodies enter infected body cells and destroy them. Why is this wrong?
cards.back: Antibodies do not enter infected cells. **Cytotoxic T lymphocytes** recognise infected body cells displaying a matching antigen and destroy them.
cards.hint: Which cell type does the destroying?

cards.front: Why is a second infection by the same pathogen often dealt with faster?
cards.back: Some activated **B and T lymphocytes** become memory cells that remain after the infection. They enable a faster response to the same antigen later.
Protection against broad groups of pathogens, responding to **common features** without selecting a uniquely matching lymphocyte. Barriers and innate responses are examples.

cards.front: How do innate and adaptive responses work together?
cards.back: Innate cells can **present antigens** to T lymphocytes, and antibodies from the adaptive response can help phagocytes engulf pathogens.
cards.hint: Name one way each direction helps.
